subject: math
cluster: Experiment with transformations in the plane
description: Students develop and apply precise definitions of the three rigid motions in terms of geometric primitives rather than coordinate shortcuts. A translation is defined by a directed line segment (vector): every point $P$ moves so that $\overrightarrow{PP'}$ is parallel to, the same length as, and the same direction as the defining vector. A reflection across a line $m$ sends each point $P$ to the point $P'$ such that $m$ is the perpendicular bisector of $\overline{PP'}$ (points on $m$ are fixed). A rotation of $\theta$ degrees about a center $C$ sends each point $P$ to $P'$ so that $CP=CP'$ (they lie on a circle centered at $C$) and $m\angle PCP'=\theta$. Students articulate these definitions, justify why each motion preserves distance and angle measure, and use the definitions to locate images, identify centers and lines, and decide whether a description actually specifies a rigid motion.
subSkills: State the definition of a translation in terms of a directed line segment: $\overline{PP'}$ is parallel to and congruent to the defining segment with the same direction
State the definition of a reflection across line $m$: $m$ is the perpendicular bisector of $\overline{PP'}$ for every off-line point $P$, and points on $m$ are fixed
State the definition of a rotation about center $C$ through angle $\theta$: $CP=CP'$ and $m\angle PCP'=\theta$ (image lies on the circle of radius $CP$ centered at $C$)
Identify which geometric primitive (parallel lines/segments, perpendicular bisector, circle and central angle) is the defining feature of each motion
Locate the image of a point under a given translation, reflection, or rotation using the definition (perpendicular bisector, equal radii, central angle)
Recover the parameters of a motion from a preimage and image: the translation vector, the reflection line, or the center and angle of a rotation
Explain why each rigid motion preserves distance and angle measure (carries segments to congruent segments and angles to congruent angles)
Distinguish a fully specified rigid motion from an underspecified or non-rigid description (e.g., a center without an angle, or a 'stretch' that changes length)

problemArchetypes.name: Match motion to defining primitive
problemArchetypes.example: Which rigid motion is defined by the condition that the line of the motion is the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining each point to its image? Answer: a reflection.

problemArchetypes.name: Complete the definition
problemArchetypes.example: Fill in: 'A rotation about center $C$ through angle $\theta$ maps point $P$ to $P'$ so that $CP = \underline{\quad}$ and $m\angle PCP' = \underline{\quad}$.' Answer: $CP'$ and $\theta$.

problemArchetypes.name: Locate image from the definition
problemArchetypes.example: Point $P$ is reflected across line $m$. If the foot of the perpendicular from $P$ to $m$ is $F$ and $PF = 3$, then $P'$ lies on ray opposite $\overrightarrow{FP}$ with $FP' = 3$, so $m$ is the perpendicular bisector of $\overline{PP'}$ and $PP' = 6$.

problemArchetypes.name: Translation by a directed segment
problemArchetypes.example: Under the translation along directed segment $\overrightarrow{AB}$ with $AB = 5$, the image $P'$ of any point $P$ satisfies $\overrightarrow{PP'}$ parallel to $\overrightarrow{AB}$, same direction, and $PP' = 5$.

problemArchetypes.name: Recover the parameters of the motion
problemArchetypes.example: A point $P$ maps to $P'$ under a rotation about $C$. Given $CP = CP' = 4$ and $m\angle PCP' = 90^\circ$, the motion is a $90^\circ$ rotation about $C$; the perpendicular bisector of $\overline{PP'}$ passes through $C$.

problemArchetypes.name: Justify distance/angle preservation
problemArchetypes.example: Explain why a reflection across $m$ preserves the length of $\overline{PQ}$. Since $m$ is the perpendicular bisector of both $\overline{PP'}$ and $\overline{QQ'}$, congruent right triangles give $P'Q' = PQ$.

problemArchetypes.name: Decide if a description specifies a rigid motion
problemArchetypes.example: Does 'rotate the figure about point $C$' fully specify a rotation? No. A rotation requires both a center and a directed angle $\theta$; the angle is missing, so the image is not determined.

Easy.description: Single-step recall and recognition. The student names the rigid motion tied to a given defining primitive, or fills one blank in a stated definition. No construction or computation beyond reading the definition.
constraints: Identify the motion from its defining feature (perpendicular bisector to reflection, circle and central angle to rotation, parallel congruent segment to translation)
Complete a single blank in a definition (e.g., supply $CP'$ or $\theta$)
Match each of translation, reflection, rotation to the primitive it uses
No image points must be located; the defining condition is stated directly in the prompt

Medium.description: Apply one definition to locate an image point or to read off one parameter. The student uses the perpendicular-bisector condition, equal radii with a central angle, or the directed-segment condition to compute a length, an angle, or a single coordinate-free position.
constraints: Use the reflection definition to find a distance such as $PP' = 2\,PF$ given the distance $PF$ to the line
Use the rotation definition to state $CP' = CP$ and $m\angle PCP' = \theta$ for a specific $\theta$ such as $60^\circ$, $90^\circ$, or $180^\circ$
Use the translation definition to find $PP'$ from the length of the directed segment
Recover exactly one parameter (the reflection line as perpendicular bisector, the translation length, or the rotation radius) from given data

Hard.description: Multi-step reasoning, full parameter recovery, or justification. The student recovers a complete motion from preimage and image, explains why a motion preserves distance or angle using the definition, or judges whether a description is a valid rigid motion and corrects it.
constraints: Given preimage and image data, identify the motion and all of its parameters (center and angle, line of reflection, or vector)
Justify distance or angle preservation from the definition (congruent triangles from the perpendicular bisector, or $CP = CP'$ and $CQ = CQ'$ with a shared angle for rotations)
Determine whether a verbal description fully specifies a rigid motion and state the missing element or why a 'stretch'/'dilation' is excluded
May chain two facts, e.g. find the rotation angle from $m\angle PCP'$ and then conclude $\triangle PCQ \cong \triangle P'CQ'$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Confuses which primitive defines which motion (e.g., thinks a reflection is defined by a central angle or a rotation by a perpendicular bisector)
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Names a rotation as the motion in which the line is the perpendicular bisector of $\overline{PP'}$, instead of a reflection

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Thinks the line of reflection bisects $\overline{PP'}$ but is not perpendicular to it (drops the right-angle condition)
commonMisconceptions.distractor: States only that $m$ passes through the midpoint of $\overline{PP'}$, omitting that $m \perp \overline{PP'}$, so the reflection is not actually defined

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Forgets the equal-radius condition for a rotation, keeping only the angle
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Defines a rotation by $m\angle PCP' = \theta$ alone and lets $CP' \ne CP$, which would not preserve distance

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Believes a translation can change the length or direction of the displacement segment
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Says the image $P'$ satisfies $\overrightarrow{PP'}$ parallel to the vector but with a different length, or in the opposite direction, instead of congruent and same direction

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Halves or doubles the wrong quantity when using the perpendicular-bisector definition
commonMisconceptions.distractor: For $PF = 3$ from the line of reflection, reports $PP' = 3$ instead of $PP' = 6$, treating $PF$ as the full distance to the image

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Confuses the rotation angle with the angle's supplement or with $m\angle PCP'$ being measured at the wrong vertex
commonMisconceptions.distractor: For a $60^\circ$ rotation reports $m\angle PCP' = 120^\circ$, using the supplement instead of the rotation angle

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Believes a center alone (without an angle) or a line direction alone fully specifies a rigid motion
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Claims 'rotate about $C$' determines a unique image, ignoring that the angle $\theta$ is required

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Treats a dilation or stretch as a rigid motion because it 'moves' the figure
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Classifies a dilation about $C$ by scale factor $2$ as a rigid motion, ignoring that it multiplies distances and is not distance-preserving
